text: ity and treatment failure than BMT although relapse rates were similar; advanced disease status and use of colony-stimu- lating factor were also associated with poorer outcome.7 Use of umbilical cord blood is associated with slightly de- layed engraftment,2,11-13 and hence, perhaps, an increased risk of fatal infection,2,11 but a lower risk2,12,14 of graft-ver- sus-host disease (see below). A meta-analysis15 confirmed these findings, but found a similar relapse rate, and equiv- alent survival for cord blood transplantation compared with unrelated BMT. It has mainly been used for trans- plants in children, since the total number of stem cells in a donation often falls short of the levels deemed necessary for engraftment in an adult.1,2,5,13 However, cord blood is increasingly used for transplants in adults.16 Since cell dose correlated with outcome in most studies, strategies have been developed to increase progenitor cell numbers in the cord blood units; techniques include pooled or se- quential cord blood transplantation, or expansion of the cord blood cells with cytokines. Combination cord blood and bone marrow transplants, and reduced intensity regi- mens are under investigation.16-18 With autologous HSCT problems of compatibility do not arise, but if abnormal cell clones are present in the marrow (as in leukaemia) or stem cells they may be transferred back into the patient and cause disease relapse.1 Alloge- neic HSCT requires immunosuppression for about 6 months19 to prevent graft-versus-host disease (see below) until a new immunological balance is achieved. The patient is normally prepared by conditioning with to- tal body irradiation, or myeloablative chemotherapy with drugs such as cyclophosphamide or busulfan, or more of- ten both, in order to destroy host bone marrow cells.5,20 In autologous procedures, harvesting of bone marrow or pe- ripheral blood must be carried out before conditioning. Bone marrow is aspirated from the donor, and infused into the recipient via an indwelling catheter or directly into a peripheral vein. Peripheral blood stem cells are collected by cell separation after mobilisation, which is best achieved by a combination of chemotherapy and granulo- cyte or granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating fac- tor.1,2,5 Infection is a major cause of morbidity and mortal- ity after transplantation, so prophylactic cover with antimicrobials2,21,22 and normal immunoglobulins is rec- ommended,21 although the value of the latter has been questioned.23 Granulocyte colony-stimulating factors are sometimes used after allogeneic transplants to hasten hae- matopoietic recovery.
